text: Good evening. My name is Guo. I chair the association at {homeCenter}, and I have had the keys to our building for twenty-six years. $ I am not surprised by what is coming from Washington. Every few years someone needs a group to point at, and we are easy to point at. My teachers heard the same speeches when they arrived. $ [neutral] Since Monday, old people have come to our office with papers that are perfectly fine, asking what to do. We gave them a lawyer's number, a lawyer whose mother sent her to our Saturday school. That is what a community is for. I don't ask the governor to look after us. I ask the governor to leave us room to look after our own.

You asked what the state could do for neighbourhoods like ours. Honestly, less than people hope. In 2009 the city paid for an English class in our building. Two years, a very good teacher. Then the budget moved, and one Tuesday forty students stood in my hallway asking me where she went. $ So: if you fund us, fund us without strings, and let the people who built the hall decide how it is run. Don't send a man with a report. $ [warm] And to the young people here. Speeches change, presidents change. The hall will still be here if you put your time into it. Come on Thursdays. Learn who does the books. That is how you protect yourselves.

Good evening. My name is Guo. I chair the association at {homeCenter}. $ Everybody is happy about the new president, and I'm glad for them. But I want to say where he came from. Last spring we registered four hundred voters in our building, between the soup and the oranges. The Korean church did the same, and the Vietnamese association. We did not wait for anyone to notice us. We counted ourselves, and we voted together. $ [warm] That is why Washington talks differently now. Not because someone downtown discovered we exist. Because a community that sticks together can be counted, and anyone who can count has to listen.

You asked what we want from the next governor. Respect for what we built. Our Saturday school was here under six presidents and will be here after this one. If the state has money, good, we will use it. But I will not move the school into a program that ends when the program ends. $ Programs come from outside and go back outside. Power stays where people stay. $ [warm] So my real answer is for the young ones in this room. Spend your Saturdays with us. Sit on a committee. Learn the names. The next governor will listen to us exactly as long as we are many, and we are together.
Two doors, you say. Fine. Only make sure one of them is ours, and that you come through it more than once a month.
Become part of the town as it is. The town as it is did not build our hall; we did. Remember that the day they forget your name.
Good. Thursdays at seven. Mrs. Ho will show you the books, and you will not be bored, whatever she tells you.
Listening is how my old teacher found me my first job. Come and listen on a Thursday, at the hall.
Thank you. A young person with opinions. Bring them to the hall, where they count.
